paras: The attempted lynching of Zeph Davis took place at Forest, Illinois, a Wabash railroad station about sixty miles south of Chicago, on February 28, 1888, when a crowd of farmers tried to seize Davis, a young man the papers called a "mulatto," from the marshal who had captured him. Davis was accused of killing fifteen-year-old Maggie Gaughan in a Chicago factory the day before; the marshal kept him from the crowd until a train carried him back to the city. The New York Sun printed the only detailed account of the scene at Forest, while other dispatches said only that Davis "narrowly escaped lynching in the country."

Maggie Gaughan was killed with a hatchet on Monday morning, February 27, at the Greene Brothers boot-heel factory in Chicago, where Davis worked. Davis hid until evening, rode a freight train south on the Wabash road, and slept in the depot at Forest, where Marshal Martin watched him.

According to the Sun's Chicago dispatch, Martin received a description of the wanted man after Davis had left on foot and set out after him with three men on a hand car. Davis fled across the prairie and fell exhausted after nearly a mile, and the marshal took him at the point of a revolver; on the way back he confessed to the killing.

The depot was "crowded with excited farmers" when the hand car returned, and there was a rush to seize the prisoner before the marshal got him into the baggage room and shackled him. The Sun wrote that the farmers had been "clamoring to lynch him" for three hours by the time he was put aboard the evening passenger train with the marshal at his side. When Davis raised the car window and spat among the crowd, one farmer drew a long knife and lunged at him; the blade shattered the pane but missed him, and the train pulled out.

Because an "immense crowd" was waiting at Chicago's Polk street depot, Davis was taken off at the Twenty-second street station and driven in a closed carriage to the Central Station. Earlier that day some 5,000 men and boys had searched a Chicago district for him, driving Black residents into the streets; two Black boys who resembled him were "nearly killed" before word of the capture dispersed the crowd.

The next morning more than a dozen policemen rushed Davis to the coroner's inquest without stopping, to give the Gaughan family's angry friends no chance at "Lynch" attempts, the Illinois Staats-Zeitung reported. The inquest physician found no sign of an attempted assault, and the coroner's jury recommended trial, adding that the firm's employment of Black and white workers of both sexes together offended public morals.

A grand jury indicted Davis for murder on March 1, and in early April a jury found him guilty and fixed the penalty at death. A motion for a new trial was entered and denied, and the hanging was set for May 12. No report of any arrest of the crowd at Forest appears in the coverage.

Chicago dispatches carried the story to papers from Washington to California. Most printed Davis's confession and said nothing about Forest; the Sacramento Daily Record-Union added a single line on the near-lynching, and a capture bulletin in the Macon Beacon and the Hillsboro News-Herald said he had "assaulted and murdered" the girl.

The Sun's account, under the deck "Farmers Try to Lynch Him," called Davis "the bullet-headed mulatto murderer" and reported the knife attack without comment. Other headlines named him "A Brute" and "The Black Murderer"; a later one read "He's a Very Bad Coon."

The German-language Illinois Staats-Zeitung called Davis a "Scheusal" (monster), yet in an April editorial it argued that only his being Black explained the speed of his prosecution, five weeks from crime to sentence, set against the slow handling of a white man who had shot a Chinese peddler.

The capture bulletin gave Davis's age as twenty, while Davis said he was seventeen, which the Sun and other dispatches doubted. It also reported a criminal assault on the girl, which Davis denied and the inquest physician's testimony did not support.

accounts.label: Sun's Chicago dispatch
accounts.gist: Marshal and three men caught Davis on the prairie; excited farmers rushed to seize him at the depot, clamored for three hours to lynch him, and one lunged at him with a knife through the train window.

accounts.label: Wire brief
accounts.gist: Davis was captured at 'Forest Hill' and 'narrowly escaped lynching in the country.'

accounts.label: Confession wire
accounts.gist: Davis's account of the killing and flight to Forest; no mention of any crowd.

accounts.label: Illinois Staats-Zeitung (inquest report)
accounts.gist: Heavy police guard took Davis to the inquest to prevent 'Lynch' attempts by friends of the Gaughan family; the jury found he killed her and recommended trial.

framing.detail: The Sun headlined 'Farmers Try to Lynch Him,' called Davis 'the bullet-headed mulatto murderer' and told the knife lunge as a dramatic incident, without condemning the crowd.
Most papers ran the confession wire under headlines like 'A Brute's Confession' and 'The Black Murderer,' with at most one line on the near-lynching.
A capture bulletin headed 'Arrest of a Ravisher and Murderer' reported assault as fact.
'He's a Very Bad Coon' headline over the report of his feigned fit.
The Staats-Zeitung called Davis a monster but editorialized that only his race explained how fast he was tried and condemned.

conflicts.note: Forest appears in most dispatches, including the detailed Sun account; 'Forest Hill' is a single wire.
Ages come from Davis's claim and from a first-day bulletin.

versions.value: killed her, denied assault; inquest physician found no sign of attempted assault

conflicts.note: The inquest testimony is later and sworn; the assault claim comes from the first-day bulletin.
The Watertown dispatch dated April 3 says 'last evening' and the Staats-Zeitung gives April 2; the Dakotaian dateline may be a late filing.

Attempted seizure at the depot, three hours of demands to lynch, and a knife lunge through the train window; no seizure succeeded and no siege of a jail
Farmers gathered at the Forest depot

record_check.record: said to have killed Maggie Gaughan
record_check.dossier: Accused of killing Maggie Gaughan; confessed to the killing, denied assault; later convicted

info: Capture and depot crowd at Forest, February 28, 1888 (murder in Chicago Monday, February 27)
Forest, Illinois, a station on the Wabash road about sixty miles south of Chicago ('Forest Hill' in one wire)
Zeph (Zephyr) Davis, described as a 'mulatto', 'negro' and 'colored boy'; claimed to be 17, one bulletin says 20
Accused of killing 15-year-old Maggie Gaughan with a hatchet at a Chicago factory; he confessed to the killing and denied criminal assault; early bulletins alleged assault
Farmers gathered at the Forest depot ('grangers'); one drew a knife
Davis kept in custody, convicted and sentenced to hang May 12, 1888

sources.note: Only full account of the Forest depot crowd, the knife lunge, and the Chicago manhunt; Chicago dispatch Feb. 28.
quotes: There was a rush made to seize the mulatto, but the officer finally succeeded in landing his prisoner in the baggage room of the depot, where he was shackled.
Before the train started Davis raised the window and expectorated among the farmers who for three hours had been clamoring to lynch him.
Quick as a flash one of the heavily booted grangers drew a long knife and made a lunge for the negro.
If he had alighted at the Polk street depot, where an immense crowd was awaiting his arrival, he would have been lynched in short order.
Two negro boys, who bore a striking resemblance to the murderer, were nearly killed before they could prove their identity.
